lol... um, well... first off, you already Have yeast in your gut (it's called "probiotics", different than baking and brewing yeast but a micro-organisim all the same), you eat yeast in bread/baked goods and drink it in the better beers (especially hefeweizens). Homebrewers drink it in ALL of their beer, it's not harmful in any way (has to have sugar to eat to live, can't tolerate acidic environments.. like your stomach).

As for what you're making? It's not pruno because you're not in prison (and didn't add a ton of other stuff to up the sugar content trying for a higher alcohol level). Close enough to call it cider... lol What you'll want to do at this point is just let it go until it stops bubbling (normally ~2 weeks is the shortest mine goes, others who make a lot of cider will keep it going for months at a very slow rate), or you get tired of waiting. The downside to stopping sooner is possibly less alcoholic content and a sweeter finished drink.

To clear the finished product, put it in the fridge (the back of the top shelf, that's the coldest place) for a week. This will precipitate out the Majority of the "stuff" (yeast, proteins, whatnot) to the bottom, then gently pour it into your holding container while leaving the sediment behind. You'll have a "still" cider (no carbonation) at that point. If you're feeling ballsy and don't mind risking a bomb, you can seal whatever you pour into (say, a couple cleaned out 2l soda bottles) and leave it out again. There will be some yeast left, and some sugar, it ought to force carbonate to a low level. It's nearly impossible to get a full on "sparkling" cider without forced carbonation (putting the stuff in a keg under CO2 pressure).

Oh, and if I didn't say it, yes you can absolutely drink it. It may not be Enjoyable (others have done it and like it "young", meaning shortly after made, but it may be good enough too. If you want a little sweeter, just add some normal apple juice to the glass with the cider.

Don't worry though. Humans have been consuming liquids fermented by yeasts (both intentional and not) for many thousands of years. It was the Romans who first used baking yeast to ferment their liquids... you're perfectly safe to consume it.
